missions.title: What is a time series?
missions.objective: Start with one measurement. No PromQL or SQL knowledge needed.

concepts.title: A number needs a meaning
concepts.definition: A metric describes something we measure. A sample records its value at a particular time.
concepts.analogy: A café writes “4 people waiting at 10:00”. The number, unit, and time answer different questions.
concepts.body:
The metric queue_depth tells us what is being measured: people waiting. Its value, 4, tells us how many. The timestamp tells us when the measurement was taken. Without the unit, 4 could mean people, seconds, or bytes. Without the timestamp, we cannot tell whether the measurement is current.

A sample is one observation of a series. Begin by reading it aloud: “At this time, this thing had this value.” Prometheus collects measurements at intervals called scrapes; it does not normally record every individual request as a separate event.
concepts.sql_connection: Think of one SQL row with timestamp and value columns. The column name and schema explain the unit. You do not need SQL to understand the observation: when, what, and how much.

concepts.title: Samples become a time series
concepts.definition: A time series is a sequence of samples for the same measurement identity over time.
concepts.analogy: Take a photo of the same café queue every 30 seconds. The sequence tells the story that one photo cannot.
concepts.body:
Suppose the queue has 2 people at 10:00, 4 at 10:00:30, and 6 at 10:01. These are three samples of one series. Joining the points on a chart helps us see change, but the stored measurements are the points, not a continuous movie.

A scrape is a collection attempt. Events may happen between scrapes, and a failed scrape can leave a gap. More samples mean more history for the same series; they do not automatically mean more distinct series.
concepts.sql_connection: Three SQL rows with the same metric and labels but different timestamps represent three samples of one series. ORDER BY timestamp puts them in time order; it does not combine their values.

concepts.title: Labels tell similar measurements apart
concepts.definition: A series is identified by its metric name and its complete set of labels.
concepts.analogy: Two cafés can both have a queue of 4 people. A location label tells us whose queue each value describes.
concepts.body:
An instance is one running copy of an application. queue_depth{instance="a"} and queue_depth{instance="b"} are different series, even when their values happen to match. A service label can say which application the instance belongs to. A label is descriptive text; it is not another measured value.

Changing any label changes the series identity. Changing only the value or timestamp adds another sample to the existing series. In our first lab, the metric name app_active_sessions is a complete beginner query: it asks for the available active-session series at one evaluation time.
concepts.sql_connection: Labels resemble identifying columns such as service and instance. Several rows can belong to one series when those identifying columns match. Filtering a metric name is similar to selecting rows for that measurement.

missions.title: Counters and gauges
missions.objective: Learn “how many so far?” versus “how many right now?”

concepts.title: Counter: how many so far?
concepts.definition: A counter accumulates events. It rises as events occur and may reset when the process restarts.
concepts.analogy: A café receipt counter shows how many orders have been served since the till started.
concepts.body:
If the request counter reads 100 and later reads 110, ten more requests were counted. The value 110 is a running total; it does not say “110 requests per second”. A quiet period leaves the counter unchanged. Ending a request does not subtract from a requests-served counter.

Counters are useful for events such as requests, errors, or completed jobs. Names often end in _total, but a name is a convention, not proof of correct instrumentation. Later we will turn changes in this total into a speed using rate().
concepts.sql_connection: A counter sample is like a periodically saved running total. SUM of those snapshots counts earlier events repeatedly. Counting raw event rows is a different data model from sampling a cumulative counter.

steps.explanation: This is the total already accumulated when we begin watching.

steps.explanation: Another 10 requests make the total 120. New events add to the old total.

steps.explanation: More events cause a bigger jump. The graph still stores totals, not speed.

steps.title: Ask the right question
steps.explanation: The current total answers “how many so far?”. To ask “how fast?”, compare samples over elapsed time.

concepts.mistake: Reading a counter's absolute value as throughput.

concepts.title: Gauge: how much right now?
concepts.definition: A gauge measures a current amount that can naturally increase or decrease.
concepts.analogy: The number of people currently waiting rises when someone joins and falls when someone is served.
concepts.body:
A queue of 2 people can become 4 and then 1. The drop from 4 to 1 is ordinary behavior, not a restart. Temperature, free memory, active sessions, and queue depth are examples of gauges. Some gauges can be negative when that makes sense for their unit.

Choose a gauge for a current state or balance. Choose a counter for accumulating events. For a gauge, its current value, recent average, minimum, or maximum are often useful. Applying counter rate logic to an ordinary falling gauge can produce a misleading result.
concepts.sql_connection: A gauge resembles a balance recorded at different times. Selecting the latest row reads the current balance; averaging a time window summarizes recorded balances. Treating every decrease as a reset would corrupt that meaning.

concepts.title: A restart is different from a falling gauge
concepts.definition: A counter reset starts a new accumulation period; a falling gauge describes a smaller current amount.
concepts.analogy: Restarting the café till clears its receipt counter. Serving a waiting customer only shortens the queue.
concepts.body:
Imagine counter samples 100, 115, 5, 20, 35. A reset happened between the second and third samples. Subtracting the first value from the last gives a negative answer, which cannot describe a negative number of requests. Prometheus counter functions detect decreases and adjust for resets.

The adjustment cannot recover events that were never observed before a restart. It is an estimate from available samples. Metric type is therefore a promise about what a measurement means, not just how its line looks. A gauge can happen to rise for a while without becoming a counter.
concepts.sql_connection: A SQL implementation would need explicit reset-aware delta logic, typically using LAG to inspect the previous counter sample. A simple last-minus-first calculation cannot distinguish a restart from a genuine balance decrease.

steps.explanation: The new counter rises to 20 and then 35. Each increase contributes additional events.

steps.explanation: Handle resets for counters. Do not apply this interpretation to an ordinary falling gauge.

missions.title: Histograms, one observation at a time
missions.objective: Understand durations, buckets, and cumulative counts before learning percentiles.

concepts.title: Why one average is not the whole story
concepts.definition: A histogram summarizes the distribution of many observations, such as request durations.
concepts.analogy: Two cafés can have the same average waiting time, while one occasionally makes a customer wait much longer.
concepts.body:
An observation is one event’s measured value: for example, one request took 0.42 seconds. A histogram does not normally store every original duration for later inspection. It counts observations into groups called buckets and also keeps a total count and sum.

This lets us ask how much of the traffic was fast or slow. The average uses the sum and count, but loses information about the shape and tail of the distribution. Begin with four durations and watch what is retained as they enter a histogram.
concepts.sql_connection: If SQL has raw duration rows, you can inspect every request and calculate exact sample statistics. Prometheus classic histogram buckets retain counts at boundaries instead; the original duration rows cannot be reconstructed from those counts.

options: The measured duration of one request

concepts.title: A bucket is a counting rule
concepts.definition: A histogram bucket counts observations that satisfy a boundary condition.
concepts.analogy: Imagine a sign saying “count every customer served within 0.5 seconds”. The sign defines a bucket.
concepts.body:
For a bucket with upper bound 0.5 seconds, a duration of 0.42 qualifies and a duration of 0.8 does not. The boundary is inclusive: 0.5 itself qualifies. The boundary is a duration; the bucket value is a count. Confusing those two units is a common source of errors.

A conventional histogram chart often draws separate intervals. Prometheus classic buckets instead use cumulative upper bounds. We will make that difference explicit in the next lesson. For now, follow one observation and decide which upper-bound rules it satisfies.
concepts.sql_connection: A bucket count is like COUNT(*) WHERE duration <= 0.5. The SQL predicate describes the bucket’s inclusive boundary. It is not SELECT duration, and the bucket value is not a latency measurement.

concepts.title: Prometheus buckets are cumulative
concepts.definition: A classic bucket with label le="x" counts every observation less than or equal to x.
concepts.analogy: A short person qualifies under several height limits. A fast request likewise contributes to several duration buckets.
concepts.body:
The label le means “less than or equal”. A 0.42-second observation increments the 0.5-second, 1-second, and +Inf buckets. It does not increment the 0.1-second bucket. Larger buckets include the counts already present in smaller buckets, so adding all bucket values would double-count observations.

The +Inf bucket has no finite upper limit and includes every observation. Subtract neighboring cumulative buckets to find an interval count: count(0.5 < duration <= 1) equals bucket(le=1) minus bucket(le=0.5). Cumulative means both inclusion across bounds and accumulation over events.
concepts.sql_connection: Several COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE duration <= bound) expressions reproduce cumulative buckets from raw rows. Subtract neighboring cumulative counts for a disjoint interval. Do not SUM all cumulative bucket columns to count requests.

steps.explanation: Every request still reaches +Inf. Compare neighboring counts; never add all cumulative buckets.

concepts.title: Read _bucket, _count, and _sum
concepts.definition: A classic histogram exposes bucket counters, an observation counter, and a sum of observed values.
concepts.analogy: A café ledger can retain how many orders there were, total time spent serving them, and counts below each service-time limit.
concepts.body:
The _count series counts observations; it equals the +Inf bucket. The _sum series adds their measured values. For nonnegative request durations, both behave like counters. With four durations 0.12, 0.42, 0.8, and 1.4 seconds, the count is 4 and the sum is 2.74 seconds. Their ratio is 0.685 seconds per request.

That is the mean of the accumulated observations, not a p95. Later, rate(_sum)/rate(_count) will describe a recent mean rather than a lifetime mean. Observations that can be negative need extra care because their sum may decrease.
concepts.sql_connection: Raw SQL duration rows support COUNT(*) and SUM(duration), whose ratio gives the mean. The matching Prometheus suffixes describe stored totals, not SQL operators that are automatically run at query time.

questions.prompt: What does a histogram summarize?
questions.explanation: Histograms summarize the spread of measurements such as durations.

questions.prompt: What does le="0.5" mean?
options: Duration less than or equal to 0.5 seconds
questions.explanation: le names the inclusive upper bound; the bucket value is a count.

questions.prompt: A 0.42s observation affects 0.1s, 0.5s, 1s, +Inf buckets how?
questions.explanation: Classic buckets are cumulative; all containing bounds receive the observation.

questions.prompt: What does the +Inf bucket count?
questions.explanation: Every observation lies below the unbounded +Inf upper limit.

questions.prompt: How do you count observations in (0.5s, 1s]?
questions.explanation: Subtracting nested cumulative counts isolates that interval.

questions.prompt: Which equals the +Inf bucket count?
questions.explanation: _count and +Inf count the same observation population.

questions.prompt: Does _sum/_count give a p95?
questions.explanation: The mean uses total duration and count; a percentile needs distribution information.

concepts.title: One moment versus a window
concepts.definition: An instant vector has one value per selected series at an evaluation time; a range vector contains samples over a window.
concepts.analogy: An instant view is a photo of several queues now. A range vector is a short photo album for each queue.
concepts.body:
The word vector here means a collection. queue_depth selects series at one evaluation time. queue_depth[5m] supplies recent samples separately for each series, normally as input to a function. The stored metric type (counter or gauge) is different from the query’s result type (scalar, instant vector, or range vector).

A range query is another idea: it evaluates an expression repeatedly at multiple times to draw a chart. A range vector is an expression’s time-window input. Real instant selectors also use lookback and staleness rules, so “latest usable sample” need not mean a sample with exactly the evaluation timestamp.
concepts.sql_connection: A snapshot table resembles one instant view. Timestamp-filtered history resembles a range-vector input. A chart runs calculations at many times; that is different from merely returning one set of historical rows.

concepts.title: Filter labels before doing arithmetic
concepts.definition: Label matchers select the series whose descriptive labels satisfy your conditions.
concepts.analogy: Before comparing queues, choose the café location and the till you actually want to study.
concepts.body:
up{service="api"} selects the availability series whose service label equals api. Commas inside braces mean AND. The matchers = and != compare exact label strings; =~ and !~ use regular expressions. Prometheus label regexes are fully anchored, so =~"api" matches the entire value api rather than api-server.

A matcher that accepts an empty string can also match a missing label. This is not automatically the same as SQL NULL behavior. Filtering changes which series are considered; it does not change their measured values.

concepts.title: A window has exact boundaries
concepts.definition: A PromQL range selector includes the right boundary and excludes the left boundary.
concepts.analogy: A “last minute” album at 10:01 includes the 10:01 photo, but not the photo exactly at 10:00.
concepts.body:
At evaluation time t, [5m] selects samples where timestamp is greater than t minus five minutes and less than or equal to t. As evaluation time moves, old samples leave the window and new ones enter. Each series gets its own window.

This matters when calculating averages or rates near a boundary. A duration tells us how far back to look, not how many samples are guaranteed to exist. Scrape failures and different scrape intervals change the sample count. Begin with visible dots and mark which ones are included before calculating anything.
concepts.sql_connection: The corresponding SQL time predicate is timestamp > t - window AND timestamp <= t. BETWEEN includes both ends and therefore needs care when matching this particular PromQL rule.

missions.title: From totals to speed
missions.objective: Build rate(), irate(), and increase() from visible counter changes.

concepts.title: Change divided by time is a speed
concepts.definition: A per-second rate measures how quickly a counter increases, not how large its total is.
concepts.analogy: An odometer tells distance traveled. Speed compares the change in distance with the time it took.
concepts.body:
If a counter rises by 30 requests over 15 seconds, the observed interval speed is 30 / 15 = 2 requests per second. Dividing by the number of samples would use the wrong denominator: samples are observations, not seconds. A larger historical counter can still be growing more slowly than a smaller one.

PromQL rate(counter[window]) estimates a per-second increase using the selected samples, reset handling, and boundary extrapolation. The animation begins with the simple change-over-time idea. The later lessons explain why the real function is more careful than subtracting two arbitrary values.
concepts.sql_connection: LAG(value) and timestamp differences can calculate observed adjacent deltas in SQL. This is an intuition for rate, not a full implementation of Prometheus reset handling and extrapolation.

concepts.title: rate() and irate() look at different evidence
concepts.definition: rate() estimates average increase across a window; irate() uses only the latest two samples in that window.
concepts.analogy: Average trip speed and the speed between your last two roadside markers can disagree during a sudden acceleration.
concepts.body:
Use the same counter samples: 100, 110, 120, 130, 190 at 15-second intervals. The last interval adds 60 requests in 15 seconds: irate is 4 requests/second. Across the first-to-last observed span, the increase is 90 over 60 seconds: 1.5 requests/second. In this example a 75-second window ending at the last sample gives rate=1.5 after its boundary extrapolation.

The [75s] window still matters to irate: it must contain the two samples, but irate does not average all of them. rate is generally steadier for alerts; irate responds more sharply to the last interval. Both are counter functions and both handle resets.
concepts.sql_connection: Compare an average of reset-aware changes across a window with the delta between the last two ordered samples. SQL LAG is useful for adjacent changes, but a full Prometheus rate implementation needs additional boundary and reset logic.

concepts.title: Handle resets before combining counters
concepts.definition: Counter functions adjust observed decreases so a restart is not mistaken for negative event traffic.
concepts.analogy: Add up the receipts from before and after the till restart, rather than subtracting the new till display from the old one.
concepts.body:
For samples 100, 115, 5, 20, 35, the observed reset-adjusted changes are 15, 5, 15, and 15: a total of 50. The unknown activity between the last old-process scrape and the restart cannot be reconstructed perfectly. Counter functions work from available observations.

Keep each original instance separate while calculating rate. If you sum counters first, another instance’s increase can hide one instance’s reset. At the aggregation level later in this course we will combine the resulting rates. Gauge calculations must not treat ordinary decreases this way.
concepts.sql_connection: A reset-aware SQL delta can use CASE WHEN value >= previous THEN value-previous ELSE value END for nonnegative counters. This demonstrates the observed-change adjustment, but still omits Prometheus boundary extrapolation.

concepts.title: increase() answers “how many during this window?”
concepts.definition: increase() estimates the counter increase over the full selected window, while rate() expresses it per second.
concepts.analogy: “Two orders per second” is a speed. “About 120 orders in a minute” is a quantity over an interval.
concepts.body:
For counters, increase(x[window]) is rate(x[window]) multiplied by the window duration in seconds. Prometheus extrapolates toward the window boundaries when samples do not land exactly on them, subject to its extrapolation rules. Therefore the result may be fractional even when the underlying events are whole requests.

In the 75-second animation example, rate is 1.5 requests/second and increase is 112.5 requests. The observed first-to-last change is only 90 across 60 seconds; the additional amount is a boundary estimate, not an extra stored sample. This distinction is why “last minus first” is not always exact increase().
concepts.sql_connection: SQL SUM of reset-aware adjacent deltas estimates observed change. Matching increase exactly also requires Prometheus extrapolation and its treatment of boundary gaps. Multiplying an accurate per-second rate by a duration changes the unit to events.

lab.goal: Calculate the recent per-second rate for each original request-counter series using a five-minute window.
lab.sql: WITH d AS (SELECT service, instance, status, value, LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY service, instance, status ORDER BY timestamp) AS prev FROM samples WHERE metric='http_requests_total' AND timestamp BETWEEN (SELECT MAX(timestamp)-300 FROM snapshot) AND (SELECT MAX(timestamp) FROM snapshot)) SELECT service, instance, status, SUM(CASE WHEN value>=prev THEN value-prev ELSE value END)/300 AS observed_rate FROM d WHERE prev IS NOT NULL GROUP BY service, instance, status;
lab.hint: Give rate() the counter name followed by a [5m] range. Keep the original series separate.
lab.equivalence: The SQL estimates observed reset-aware changes. Prometheus also extrapolates at range boundaries; exact equality is not promised.

missions.title: Calculate over time
missions.objective: Understand sum_over_time, avg_over_time, and the question each function answers.

concepts.title: sum_over_time() adds samples, not new events
concepts.definition: sum_over_time() adds the sampled values inside each series’s selected time window.
concepts.analogy: If three queue photos show 2, 4, and 6 people, adding the photo counts gives 12—not necessarily 12 different people.
concepts.body:
sum_over_time(queue_depth[90s]) computes one sum per queue series. In our teaching example, the selected values 2, 4, 6 sum to 12. This is a sum of snapshots: the same waiting person could appear in multiple photos. It is not automatically a count of arrivals, nor a time integral.

More frequent scrapes can increase the sum even when the real-world situation is unchanged. Adding samples of a cumulative counter is especially misleading for event counts because earlier events are repeated in later totals. Use increase on a counter when you want interval event counts.
concepts.sql_connection: For one series, this is SUM(value) over timestamp-filtered rows. It adds measured snapshots. To count raw events in SQL you would need event rows, a different table from sampled metric values.

concepts.title: avg_over_time() describes the average sample
concepts.definition: avg_over_time() gives each selected sample equal weight when averaging its values.
concepts.analogy: Average the queue sizes in your photos: (2 + 4 + 6) / 3 = 4 people per sampled moment.
concepts.body:
For three selected gauge samples 2, 4, 6, the average is 4. The divisor is the number of included samples, not the duration in seconds. This can answer “what did this gauge typically look like in the observations we collected?”

Prometheus gives each sample equal weight, even when samples are not evenly spaced. It is not automatically a time-weighted average or an integral. For counters, averaging the accumulated totals still does not tell us how many new events occurred. Match the function to the metric’s meaning and to the exact question.
concepts.sql_connection: AVG(value) over the corresponding rows is an equal-sample average. SQL can also implement a duration-weighted average, but that is a different calculation and should be labeled separately.

concepts.title: Minimum, maximum, and sample count
concepts.definition: min_over_time, max_over_time, and count_over_time answer three different questions about a series window.
concepts.analogy: From queue photos, ask for the shortest queue, the longest queue, or simply how many photos you managed to take.
concepts.body:
For samples 2, 4, 6, min_over_time is 2, max_over_time is 6, and count_over_time is 3. The first two retain the gauge’s unit; count_over_time reports a number of samples. It does not count requests or people passing through the system.

An unexpected sample count can help you investigate collection gaps, provided you know the expected scrape interval. Missing observations can also hide a peak between scrapes, so max_over_time means the largest observed sample, not proof of the largest value that ever existed.

concepts.title: Gauge change is not counter rate
concepts.definition: delta() estimates a gauge’s change across a window; deriv() estimates its per-second linear trend.
concepts.analogy: A queue shrinking is real improvement, not a reset that should be corrected into positive growth.
concepts.body:
For a gauge, a negative change is meaningful. delta(queue_depth[5m]) estimates the difference across the full window using boundary extrapolation. deriv(queue_depth[5m]) fits a straight-line trend to float samples and reports a slope per second. Both need enough samples to make their calculation meaningful.

Unlike rate, these functions are intended for gauge-style changes. lab.goal: Calculate the five-minute request rate per service, handling each original counter before aggregation.

WITH deltas AS (
  SELECT service, instance, status, value,
    LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY service, instance, status ORDER BY timestamp) AS prev
  FROM samples
  WHERE metric = 'http_requests_total'
    AND timestamp BETWEEN (SELECT MAX(timestamp)-300 FROM snapshot)

concepts.title: What p95 actually means
concepts.definition: The 95th percentile is a value at or below which roughly 95% of the observation population lies.
concepts.analogy: Line up 100 customer wait times from shortest to longest and find the boundary around the 95th position.
concepts.body:
Classic histograms retain bucket counts rather than raw durations. histogram_quantile estimates a percentile inside the bucket containing the desired rank. With cumulative counts 20,60,90,100 at bounds 0.1,0.5,1,2 seconds, the 95th observation lies in the 1-to-2-second bucket. Linear interpolation estimates 1.5 seconds.

That interpolation assumes a distribution inside the bucket; it does not reveal the exact original 95th duration. Wide buckets limit precision. A tail percentile describes a population, not a promise that every request will finish within that time.

concepts.title: Subqueries and recording rules reuse calculations
concepts.definition: A subquery samples an expression over time; a recording rule saves an expression’s results periodically.
concepts.analogy: You can repeatedly calculate a service total for an album, or keep writing that total into a reusable log.
concepts.body:
A subquery such as (sum(queue_depth))[5m:30s] evaluates the inner expression on a repeated time grid, producing a range of calculated results. The 30s part is the subquery resolution, not the scrape interval. An outer function can summarize those calculated samples.

A recording rule periodically stores the result of a useful expression as a new series. It can reduce repeated query work, but its rule interval and labels affect interpretation. Deep or broad subqueries can be expensive; inspect the data volume and prefer clear, reusable calculations.
concepts.sql_connection: A subquery resembles deriving a time-indexed relation and then applying another calculation. A recording rule resembles a periodically refreshed materialized result, with explicit refresh timing and dimensions.

concepts.title: An alert window is not an alert hold timer
concepts.definition: An expression chooses evidence; an alert’s for duration controls how long a condition must remain active before firing.
concepts.analogy: A café might inspect the last five minutes of service, but call for help only after a problem persists for another two minutes.
concepts.body:
A rate(...[5m]) expression looks backward over five minutes at each evaluation. An alert rule with for: 2m waits for its condition to remain active across rule evaluations before firing. These two durations have different jobs. Pending means the condition is active but the hold duration has not yet been satisfied.

If the condition stops being active during the pending period, the hold timer normally resets. Missing data may remove a vector element entirely; handle absence deliberately rather than assuming it behaves like a numeric zero. A useful alert should identify an actionable symptom and the affected service.

missions.title: Explain an incident with evidence
missions.objective: Combine the fundamentals into a careful reliability investigation.

concepts.title: Read traffic, errors, latency, and availability together
concepts.definition: An incident explanation uses several compatible signals rather than one alarming number.
concepts.analogy: A long café queue might reflect a rush of customers, slower service, a broken till, or several causes together.
concepts.body:
Start by checking the population and time window. Throughput comes from request-counter rates; error fraction compares aligned error and total rates; latency comes from the request-duration distribution; up describes scrape availability. These signals answer related but different questions.

A rising error count can simply accompany more traffic, while an error fraction reveals how large the affected share is. A latency percentile can change even when the average stays similar. None of these alone proves a root cause. Compare normal and incident scenarios, form a hypothesis, and look for evidence that could disprove it.

concepts.title: An SLO defines the reliability goal
concepts.definition: A service-level objective states the desired share of good events over a specified period.
concepts.analogy: A café promises that at least 999 of every 1,000 orders meet its success criterion over the agreed reporting period.

A 99.9% success SLO allows a bad-event fraction of 0.1%, or 0.001. Define good and bad events precisely, including which requests belong in the denominator. An availability or latency objective can use a different definition of good, so do not mix them without explanation.

A monthly objective is evaluated over its reporting period. A short five-minute error spike can threaten the budget, but does not by itself establish that the monthly SLO has already been violated. Window, population, and units remain as important here as in the very first metric lesson.
concepts.sql_connection: An SLO calculation is a carefully defined numerator divided by a denominator over an agreed interval. Filtering the two populations differently can produce a mathematically valid ratio that answers the wrong business question.

concepts.title: Programs, processes, and services
concepts.explanation:
A program is a set of instructions. A process is a running instance with resources such as memory. A service provides a capability to callers. A purchase request may involve a checkout service, payment service, and database. Each does part of the work, and a failure in one part can affect the user's result.

We will first draw that journey, then collect evidence about it. The UI experiment uses real instrumentation for logical services in one Python process. The HTTP example later adds actual network boundaries.

concepts.example: Click Buy → checkout → payment → database → response. The user sees one outcome even though several operations contributed.

concepts.title: Logs, metrics, and traces

A log records an event with context. A metric summarizes a numerical observation, often over many operations. A trace connects operations belonging to a request's journey. These signals answer different but related questions: what happened, how much or how often, and where a particular request spent its work.

A count cannot show the full story of one request. A single trace cannot describe the entire population's error rate. Use the signals together rather than forcing one to answer every question.

concepts.title: A span is one operation
concepts.explanation:
A span represents an operation with a start, end, name, identifiers, and optional attributes, events, and status. A trace groups related spans. A root span has no parent in the recorded trace; child spans identify the operation that caused them. This makes the request's structure visible.

Meaningful names describe bounded operations such as a route or database operation. A span does not have to represent an entire service. One service may create many spans, while missing instrumentation may leave important work unobserved.
concepts.analogy: A trip contains legs; a trace contains operations represented as spans.
concepts.example: POST /checkout is the root operation. charge is a child, and SELECT inventory is a child of charge in the propagated experiment.
concepts.mistake: Counting spans is not the same as counting user requests: one request can generate many spans.

concepts.title: Context is more than a variable name
concepts.explanation:
Context carries information about the current operation across execution boundaries. Creating a span in the caller does not automatically make a remote service its child. A carrier can be HTTP headers or another supported transport representation. Our UI demonstrates W3C trace-context injection and extraction in dictionaries with isolated receiver contexts. The HTTP example demonstrates actual headers crossing a network boundary.

concepts.title: API, SDK, and exporter
concepts.explanation:
An API defines how application code requests telemetry operations. An SDK implements recording and processing behavior. An exporter moves recorded data to a destination. A provider creates instrumentation objects such as tracers and meters with the configured behavior.

The experiment creates explicit providers so each run is isolated. It uses the actual Python SDK and in-memory exporters rather than inventing span IDs in the UI. In-memory export is useful for learning and testing, but it is not durable backend storage.

concepts.title: A counter counts additions
concepts.explanation:
A counter records nonnegative additions to a quantity such as completed requests. It describes accumulation, while a rate describes change over a time interval. Backend temporality determines how accumulated data is represented across exports. A restart or reset must be considered by a query system when interpreting cumulative values.

Our SDK counter receives one addition per attempted checkout, with a bounded outcome label. The same experiment records successful or failed attempts rather than pretending a failed attempt never occurred. Define what is counted before interpreting a number.

concepts.mistake: Do not use a cumulative request counter as if it were the number of currently active requests.

missions.title: Sampling without losing the story

concepts.title: Head sampling chooses early
concepts.explanation:
Head sampling makes a recording decision near the beginning of a trace, before all its later outcomes are known. Probability-based sampling selects a fraction over a population; it does not guarantee exactly that fraction in a tiny batch. A lower sample rate can reduce retained trace volume while limiting the available request evidence.

Our SDK experiment uses a parent-based sampler with a trace-ID-ratio root decision. The metrics are still recorded for all attempts. Sampling traces does not automatically sample every other signal in the same way.
concepts.analogy: Selecting some passengers for a survey before the trip is different from selecting them after seeing delays.

concepts.mistake: Do not grade a sampling probability by demanding an exact count in a small random sample.

frames.narration: The decision happens before the complete outcome.
Probability is not a per-batch quota.

Observe volume and evidence quality across a meaningful population.

concepts.explanation:

It also identifies scope: in-process SDK exercise, real HTTP demo, or an actual deployed pipeline. State what was measured and what was not tested, including storage, scale, and production dependencies.

A fresh graduate should leave this course able to instrument a small Python workflow, follow its context, interpret its signals, and explain a pipeline. Production expertise additionally requires deployed-system practice, varied failure cases, operational budgets, and appropriate data policies.

concepts.example: Record: before had error spans and logs; after had connected non-error spans and successful outcomes. Timing is local execution, not a network benchmark.

glossary.metric: A numerical observation or aggregate with defined meaning.
glossary.sample: One timestamp and its measured value for a series. Example: at 10:00, queue_depth was 4 people.
glossary.unit: Quantity scale such as seconds, bytes, or degrees Celsius.
glossary.time series: The history of samples with the same metric name and complete label set.
glossary.scrape: An attempt by Prometheus to collect measurements exposed by a target at a particular time.
glossary.label: A descriptive key/value pair, such as service=api, that identifies which measurement a series represents.
glossary.instance: One running copy of an application or target. Different instances can expose separate series for the same metric.
glossary.gauge: A measured current value that can rise or fall.
glossary.counter reset: A counter starting a new accumulation period, usually after a restart. An observed decrease is handled as a reset by counter functions.
glossary.observation: A measurement with defined meaning, units, and time.
glossary.histogram: Instrument grouping observations into a distribution.
glossary.distribution: How measurements are spread across possible values: for example, how many requests are fast, medium, or slow.
glossary.bucket: A defined distribution range; representation controls count semantics.
glossary.le: The classic histogram label meaning less than or equal to. le=0.5 counts observations up to and including 0.5 in the metric's unit.
glossary.cumulative bucket: A bucket whose count includes every observation below its upper bound, including observations already counted in smaller buckets.
glossary.+Inf: An unbounded upper bucket limit. Every observation contributes to this classic histogram bucket, so it equals _count.
glossary._count: A histogram or summary's total number of observations. It does not sum their durations.
glossary._sum: The sum of observed measurement values, such as total request duration in seconds. It is not the sum of cumulative bucket counts.
glossary.instant vector: A collection containing one value for each selected series at an evaluation time.
glossary.range vector: A collection of separate series windows, each containing samples over the selected duration.
glossary.evaluation time: The timestamp at which a PromQL expression is calculated. A chart repeatedly evaluates at multiple timestamps.
glossary.selector: An expression that chooses series, usually using a metric name and optional label matchers.
glossary.matcher: A condition on a label, such as service=api, that decides whether a series is selected.
glossary.rate: Change per time interval, interpreted with reset and representation semantics.
glossary.irate: A counter's per-second increase calculated from only the latest two samples within the selected window, with reset handling.
glossary.increase: The estimated counter increase over the full selected duration. Equivalent to rate multiplied by that duration in seconds.
glossary.extrapolation: Estimating toward time-window boundaries where an exact sample may not exist. Prometheus applies specific rules and limits.
glossary.sum_over_time: Adds the selected sample values separately within each series. It does not automatically count events or unique people.
glossary.avg_over_time: Averages the selected values separately within each series, giving each sample equal weight.
glossary.min_over_time: Returns the smallest observed sample value within each selected series window.
glossary.max_over_time: Returns the largest observed sample value within each selected series window; it cannot reveal unobserved peaks.
glossary.count_over_time: Counts the samples present in each selected series window, not the events represented by counter values.
glossary.delta: Estimates a gauge's change over a selected window using boundary extrapolation. Negative changes can be meaningful.
glossary.deriv: Fits a linear regression to float gauge samples and returns the estimated slope per second.
glossary.aggregation: Combining series at an evaluation time, for example summing instance values into service totals.
glossary.by: Specifies the labels used as aggregation groups and retained on each result.
glossary.without: Removes specified labels from aggregation grouping while keeping other grouping labels.
glossary.ratio: A numerator divided by a denominator. Both must describe compatible populations, units, labels, and time windows.
glossary.bool: Changes a PromQL comparison from filtering by the condition to producing 0/1 results for matched comparisons.
glossary.vector matching: The label-key rules used to pair elements of two instant vectors for an operation.
glossary.on: Explicitly names the labels used as a vector-matching key.
glossary.ignoring: Excludes selected labels from the vector-matching key.
glossary.group_left: Permits a many-to-one arithmetic match with multiple left-side series and a unique right-side match. It is not a SQL left outer join.
glossary.missing series: A series with no usable element in the current result. It is different from a present sample whose value is zero.
glossary.absent: A function that returns an absence signal when its input has no elements. It does not automatically recreate every missing target's labels.
glossary.set operator: and, or, or unless: operations based on membership of label sets rather than arithmetic on the sample values.
glossary.percentile: Position in a distribution, often estimated from aggregated data.
glossary.quantile: A population fraction expressed from 0 to 1, such as 0.95 for the 95th percentile.
glossary.interpolation: Estimating a value between known boundaries. Classic histogram quantiles interpolate inside the bucket containing the desired rank.
glossary.native histogram: A representation using composite histogram samples rather than separate float series for each classic bucket.
glossary.summary: A metric family that can expose quantiles calculated by the application, together with observation count and sum.
glossary.offset: A modifier that shifts a selector's reference time relative to the evaluation time.
glossary.subquery: Repeated evaluation of an expression over a time grid, producing calculated samples for an outer expression.
glossary.recording rule: A rule that periodically evaluates an expression and stores its result as a new time series.
glossary.pending: An alert condition is active, but its configured hold duration has not yet been satisfied.
glossary.firing: An alert condition has satisfied its firing requirements, including the for duration when configured.
glossary.for duration: The alert-rule hold period during which a condition must remain active before firing. It differs from a query's lookback window.
glossary.cardinality: Number of distinct metric identities produced by attribute combinations.
glossary.SLO: A service-level objective: a defined target for good events over a specified population and assessment period.
glossary.error budget: The allowed share of bad events under an SLO. A 99.9% good-event target allows a bad fraction of 0.001.
glossary.burn rate: Observed bad-event fraction divided by allowed bad-event fraction. It describes budget pressure, not remaining time by itself.
glossary.process: A running program instance with resources.
glossary.request: A caller's operation sent to a service.
glossary.log: A record of an event with body and context.
glossary.trace: Related operations forming a request journey.
glossary.OpenTelemetry: A framework for producing, collecting, and exporting telemetry.
glossary.instrumentation: Code or libraries adding meaningful observations to programs.
glossary.exporter: Component sending recorded telemetry to a destination.
glossary.span: A timed operation with identifiers and optional attributes, events, and status.
glossary.parent: The related operation that caused a child span.
glossary.root span: A recorded span with no parent in the observed trace.
glossary.duration: End time minus start time for an operation.
glossary.latency: Elapsed waiting time for the defined operation.
glossary.critical path: The dependent sequence determining elapsed completion time.
glossary.span ID: Identifier of one span within a trace.
glossary.context: Information about current work carried across execution boundaries.
glossary.carrier: Transport representation such as HTTP headers holding context.
glossary.extract: Read supported context from a carrier.
glossary.traceparent: W3C header carrying trace identity, parent identity, and flags.
glossary.authorization: Permission to perform an operation, separate from trace linkage.
glossary.baggage: Propagated application-defined context needing explicit data boundaries.
glossary.API: Interface used by application code to request telemetry operations.
glossary.SDK: Implementation providing configured recording and processing behavior.
glossary.provider: Configured source of tracers, meters, or loggers.
glossary.resource: Attributes describing the entity producing telemetry.
glossary.service.name: Resource attribute identifying the producing service.
glossary.attribute: Named context attached to a resource or observation.
glossary.semantic convention: Shared defined meaning for instrumentation names and attributes.
glossary.temporality: How metric data represents accumulation across export intervals.
glossary.up-down counter: Instrument recording positive and negative changes to a quantity.
glossary.severity: Classification of a log event's importance or level.
glossary.status: Reported outcome of a span, separate from a log message.
glossary.exception: Occurrence representing a failure or exceptional condition.
glossary.event: Named occurrence attached to an operation or recorded in a log.
glossary.dependency: Another component an operation relies on.
glossary.evidence: Observations supporting or challenging a conclusion.
glossary.Collector: Component receiving, processing, and exporting telemetry through pipelines.
glossary.receiver: Collector component accepting supported telemetry input.
glossary.processor: Collector component transforming or managing pipeline data.
glossary.pipeline: Connected receiver, processor, and exporter stages for a signal.
glossary.batch: Grouping records for more efficient export with a delay tradeoff.
glossary.memory limiter: Processor helping bound memory behavior under pressure.
glossary.backpressure: Slowing or rejecting input when downstream capacity is limited.
glossary.YAML: Indented configuration format with objects, lists, and values.
glossary.sampling: Selecting trace evidence for recording or retention.
glossary.head sampling: A decision made before the complete trace outcome is known.
glossary.probability: A population selection chance rather than an exact small-sample quota.
glossary.parent-based sampling: A child decision respecting relevant parent sampling context.
glossary.tail sampling: Later retention decision using observed trace information.
glossary.redaction: An explicit transformation removing selected data from defined locations.
glossary.privacy: Controlling unnecessary data collection, propagation, and disclosure.
glossary.N+1: Repeated dependency calls for items that may admit a suitable grouped operation.
glossary.batch query: A grouped dependency operation in the teaching workload.
glossary.baseline: Comparable initial evidence before an intervention.
glossary.verification: Evidence checking the intended outcome after a change.
glossary.remediation: A response addressing a diagnosed condition.
